readerTitle: Same dishwasher, same price. Why did one seller win?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (주방설비 유통업체 두 곳과 식당, 페인트 가게, 호텔 행사 영업) + 마케팅 격언 (Levitt의 드릴과 구멍)
insight: 고객은 제품을 사지 않고, 자기 사업에서 달라질 결과를 산다. 그래서 영업은 기능이 아니라 고객의 말로 된 결과에서 시작한다.
misconception: 제품 사양과 장점을 많이 정확하게 설명할수록 더 잘 팔린다.

sources.text: Levitt, T. (1983). The Marketing Imagination. Levitt는 '1/4인치 드릴' 문장을 Leo McGinneva의 말로 소개함
Christensen, C. et al. (2005). Marketing Malpractice. Harvard Business Review. (Levitt의 드릴 격언 인용)
모든 사업 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 'People don't want a quarter-inch drill, they want a quarter-inch hole'은 흔히 Theodore Levitt의 말로 알려져 있으나 Levitt 본인은 Leo McGinneva의 말로 소개했습니다. 카드에는 'a line often credited to Theodore Levitt'으로 적었습니다. 게시 전 원문 확인 필요.
식기세척기 사이클 시간, 저녁 8시 접시 부족, 페인트 1회 도장 등은 모두 설명용 가상 설정입니다. 특정 제품의 실제 사양으로 읽히지 않도록 했습니다.

cards.title: Same dishwasher, same price. Why did one seller win?
body: Two kitchen supply distributors visit the same restaurant owner in the same week. They offer the same commercial dishwasher at the same price.
The owner signs with the second one before the visit is over. The first seller never finds out why.

image.label: Two salespeople presenting the same dishwasher to a restaurant owner
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 식당 주방에 똑같은 식기세척기 두 대가 나란히 있고, 왼쪽 영업사원은 사양표를 들고, 오른쪽 영업사원은 붐비는 저녁 식당 장면이 담긴 말풍선을 보여줌. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: How would you open the pitch?
body: You sell for a kitchen supply distributor. The owner says Friday nights are chaos: around 8 pm they run out of clean plates, and a cook leaves the line to wash by hand.
Which opening line do you lead with?

options.text: "This model runs a full rack in about 90 seconds and comes with a three-year warranty."
options.feedback: Accurate and useful, but the owner has to do the work of linking 90 seconds to Friday at 8 pm. Many won't.

options.text: "On a Friday, you'd have clean plates ready before 8 pm, and your cook stays on the line."
options.feedback: It describes their night after the purchase, in their own words. The specs then become proof, not the pitch.

options.text: "If you order this week, I can take 5% off."
options.feedback: A discount can close a deal, but it gives away margin before the owner even sees why the machine matters to them.

cards.title: The first seller sold a machine. The second sold a Friday night.
body: The first distributor walked through the spec sheet: cycle time, water use, steel grade, warranty. All true.
The second asked about the owner's busiest night first. Then she said one thing: "No more running out of plates at 8 pm, and no cook washing dishes."
The owner already knew what a lost cook costs on a full night. The second seller didn't need to explain the value. She pointed at it.

cards.title: Selling outcomes
body: **Selling outcomes** means describing the change your product makes in the customer's business or life, not just what the product is or does.

Think of three steps. A *feature* is what it has: a 90-second cycle. A *benefit* is what that does: faster washing. An **outcome** is what changes for this customer: plates ready at 8 pm, cook back on the line, tables turned on time.

image.label: Three steps: feature, benefit, outcome
image.brief: 계단 세 칸 인포그래픽. 아래부터 "Feature: 90-second cycle", "Benefit: faster washing", "Outcome: plates ready at 8 pm". 맨 위 칸을 가장 밝게 강조하고, 그 위에 웃는 식당 주인 아이콘.

cards.softwareNote: In software, "real-time dashboards" is a feature. "Your team spots a stockout before customers do" is an outcome. Buyers renew for the second, not the first.

cards.title: Customers compare the price to the outcome.
body: There's a line often credited to Theodore Levitt: people don't want a quarter-inch drill, they want a quarter-inch hole.
A buyer can't easily weigh $8,000 against "90-second cycle." They can weigh it against a cook's lost hours every Friday. **The outcome is what the price gets measured against.**
It also travels. The owner will repeat "no more running out of plates" to a business partner. Nobody repeats a cycle time.

cards.title: A paint store sells a free Saturday.
body: A paint store clerk could say, "This one has high pigment and covers in one coat."
Or the clerk could ask what the customer is painting, hear "my kid's bedroom, this weekend," and say, "You'll finish in one day and still have Sunday free."
Same can, same price. The second answer sells the weekend the customer is actually picturing.

image.label: A paint can next to a calendar with Sunday circled as free
image.brief: 페인트 통 옆에 주말 달력. 토요일에는 붓 아이콘, 일요일에는 동그라미와 해먹 아이콘. 실제 페인트 브랜드나 로고 없음. 밝고 따뜻한 색감.

cards.title: An outcome only works if it's theirs and it's true.
body: You can't name the right outcome without asking first. A generic promise like "save time and money" sounds like every other seller.
Don't promise results you can't control. If the plates still run out because the kitchen is understaffed, the outcome you sold becomes the complaint you hear.
And keep the specs ready. Technical buyers, like a head chef or an engineer, want proof. Lead with the outcome, then show the features that make it believable.

cards.title: Now you're selling a hotel's meeting space.
body: An HR lead is planning a two-day offsite for 40 managers. On the phone she says last year's offsite "ended with no decisions, because half the time went to fixing logistics."
What do you lead with?

options.text: "Our ballroom seats 200 and has new projectors and sound."
options.feedback: Impressive specs, but a room for 200 doesn't speak to a group of 40 that needs decisions. It invites a price comparison with every other hotel.

options.text: "Rooms, meals and equipment in one package, one invoice."
options.feedback: A real benefit that reduces her admin. It's close, but it stops one step short of the result she named.

options.text: "We handle the logistics so your managers leave with decisions made."
options.feedback: It answers last year's failure in her own words. The package and the equipment then become the proof that you can deliver it.

cards.title: Sell what changes for the customer, then prove it with the product.
body: Features describe your product. Outcomes describe the customer's life after buying it. Lead with the outcome, in their words.
**Try it today:** pick your top product. Write one feature, the benefit it creates, and the outcome a real customer told you about. Use that last line in your next pitch.
